utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Matovina, yesterday during the examination-in-chief you referred to Jovan Raskovic, and you said that he had a major impact on the Serb population or, rather, he was one of the founders of the Serb Democratic Party. I personally did not know him, but his statements are well known. You say that he supported the idea of a Greater Serbia, which is not true. When did Jovan Raskovic speak about a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday during my testimony, I spoke about the speeches he made when the Serb Democratic Party was being established in Slatina and beyond that, in Slavonia. I said that his speeches were such that it was quite clear that he advocated the project of creating a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him mention some Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The press wrote about that too. That was a generally known thing, what he actually advocated, that is, and what kind of speeches he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Jovan Raskovic never spoke about a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For example, in Vukovar, on the 22nd of July or during that speech that you mentioned, he said that Serbs would never take to arms or jeopardise anybody's children but that they would always be ready to jeopardise the Ustasha regime and that that claim is not anti-Croatian but anti-Ustasha. Do you remember that, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that speech of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was the content of most of his speeches that we had the opportunity of reading about in the papers or seeing in other media. So not anti-Croatian, as he said, but anti-Ustasha. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I do not know of that kind of a speech his in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that the election campaign in Croatia at the beginning of 1990 was full of various paraphernalia, pictures, et cetera, that revived the spirit of Ante Pavlic and the Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945? Do you remember that at least, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in the campaign throughout Croatia. I already said that I was in Slatina. And I was not involved in politics. I was a policeman. I said yesterday what my position was and what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what the content of this policy was as regards the attitude towards the Serbs? It was quite well known: One-third was supposed to be killed, another third was supposed to be expelled, and the remaining third should be Catholicised.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of such positions. I know that perhaps individuals said something like that but that was never the official policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember, for example, that in April 1990 - you could see that in the newspapers in Croatia - the town of Hvar one morning had graffiti saying, "Croatia all the way up to Zemun, Zemun is Croatia." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember that. I already said that I was not involved in such a chronology. I was doing my own job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that even Ivica Racan, the current Prime Minister of Croatia, on the 27th of February 1990 stated that the HDZ is a party of dangerous intentions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that statement, but statements made by politicians are statements that are used on certain occasions, as always.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember, then, that Dalibor Brozovic, one of the six members of the Presidency of the then Croatia - and the president was Franjo Tudjman - in each and every one of his speeches to the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he promised the citizens a chequerboard on Romanija and the Serb insignia on the Drina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this speech of Mr. Brozovic's, and I know very little about this, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Obviously you don't know about this. At least, that's what you say. So is it correct? Do you know at least that this red and white chequerboard was actually the flag that, after 50 years, they decided would be the flag of Croatia, and do you know that it's correct that that was the state of the Independent State -- the flag of the Independent State of Croatia during the time of Ante Pavlic and the Ustasha state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've made this point several times already. We're not going to allow you constantly to reiterate the same points.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example -- do you remember, for example, a Reuters report from the 23rd of April, 1990 about the elections? This is a report on the elections of the HDZ and they're characterised as a nationalist and a predominantly separatist party. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read Reuters really. I would not like to go into political estimates regarding elections, political parties, anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that it's precisely the region of Western Slavonia that you are from had great scars from the large scale crimes that were committed during the Second World War precisely under that flag that I referred to just now? For example, the event that occurred on the 13th of January 1994 [as interpreted], the Orthodox New Year's Eve, when there was a massacre over the Serb population and when the Ustashas from Podravska Slatina surrounded the Serb village of Kometnik near Vocin and massacred 275 inhabitants. Since you lived in Western Slavonia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: According to the translation, this is January 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that the date you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] January 1942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Matovina, in view of the fact that he lived precisely in Western Slavonia, whether these scars were in people's minds at the time when there was this revival of the Ustasha movement in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in 1949. That is to say, after the Second World War. What happened during the war is something that I learned through history. It is true that there were crimes, and that is publicly referred to, and nobody ever remained silent with regard to any one of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever remained silent about any one of these crimes? That is not true. But do you remember that in Croatia in 1990 constitutional amendments were passed? Not to go into all of them individually, but the substance was that the Serbs no longer had the status of a constituent people with these amendments. Do you remember that in 1990?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to. I think that there is a constitution and it says quite clearly what the rights of all peoples are. I would not go into an interpretation of constitutional provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember, since you were then a public figure in a way, that the Croatian authorities did not take into account any one of the Serb amendments with regard to the constitution, especially with regard to requests of the Serbs to retain in the new constitution the status that they had in all other constitutions after the Second World War, the status of a constituent people? Do you remember that, that not a single Serb amendment was adopted?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was adopted and that a compromise was found and that there is such a solution in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, is it correct that everything that happened, all these symbols that were displayed and all the way up to the illegal arming of paramilitary formations in Croatia, instigated not only nationalism but also fascism in Croatia and a disparaging attitude towards the Serbs? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's just general abuse. Yes. Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the election campaign in Croatia in 1990 unequivocally announced a pogrom attitude of these nationalist parties toward the Serbs and this way of resolving the national question in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not right, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What can you say about founding the National Guard Corps as a professional armed organisation that was anti-constitutional? I hope that you know that the Constitutional Court ruled that the establishment of this paramilitary formation was unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such ruling by the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that in Croatia in 1990 an illegal arming began?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia had to defend itself from aggression which loomed over it from day-to-day, and that turned out to be true later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these arms, ammunitions, and equipment were secretly distributed throughout the territory of Croatia and that it was distributed only to ethnic Croats, primarily members of the HDZ? Is that right or is that not right? As a policeman, you would have had to know about this.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about any kind of secret arming. You said yourself that the National Guard Corps was established, and the Croatian police later on, together with the National Guard Corps, it comprised the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That was a well-known thing throughout Yugoslavia. The Presidency of Yugoslavia, on the 9th of January, 1991, at the very beginning, passed an order to disband irregular armed formations and, at the request of the government of Croatia, they extended the deadline that was established by this order by 48 hours. That is to say that the new deadline was the 21st of January. Do you remember that and the events that followed?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. The Presidency did reach such a decision, and at the same time, the JNA armed the Serb population and prepared them for an armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the JNA was not arming anybody? They only mobilised recruits, conscripts. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during the examination-in-chief, you said that the Serbs left the police on their own, and it is well-known that it is precisely the sector of the interior that was cleansed of the Serbs by the new Croatian government, also of Croats that they thought were wrong, and that they also reinforced 18 police administrations that were then established, and they covered the territory of all of Croatia. Do you still stand by that statement of yours that it was Serbs who left the force on their own, or were they expelled from the police?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my statement. I know that nobody was dismissed. I know that nobody was expelled. I know that the police at the time was the only armed force that the Republic of Croatia had and that it was the legitimate right of the Croatian state to reinforce the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you do not know about these large-scale dismissals from public services, from the police, from the media, and even from various companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before you answer that, the question should be put: Were there large-scale dismissals, as far as you know, Mr. Matovina, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There were no dismissals. Individuals left on their own. As far as I know, where I lived and work, nobody was dismissed in accordance with the criteria that Mr. Milosevic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that in Pakrac it is precisely that the ethnic composition of the police was changed and on the 2nd of March it led to a clash between citizens who were ethnic Serbs and the police? That is in your neighbourhood. You're bound to remember that.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in my neighbourhood, and before the police station in Slatina was attacked, there was an attack on the police station in Pakrac. As for the change in the ethnic make-up, I don't know because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But if Serbs were a majority, they did not attack themselves, did they? There wasn't an attack, there was a protest.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was an attack. The police station in Pakrac was being taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croatian police, on the 17th of August, with the intention of preventing a Serb referendum from taking place, in all towns where Serbs were a majority, they tried to take away weapons, which led to the erection of roadblocks. Do you remember that, at least?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not necessary to take armaments -- arms when they were in police stations. This was just an alibi for attacks on police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement that the rebels attacked police stations in Croatia and that they wanted to take over stations where there were weapons and ammunition. Can you explain this? Does that mean that the Serbs attacked policemen and police stations where practically 85 per cent of the force was Serb? Doesn't that seem illogical to you, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the chronology of the attack on police stations yesterday, Knin, Banovina, Petrinja, Pakrac, then Obrovac, Benkovac where Serb policemen were a majority and where, after attacks were launched, the authority of the so-called SAO Krajinas was established. And after that, roadblocks were placed on roads and this area was cut off from the rest of Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, when you speak about these attacks, are you talking about attacks on police stations or are you actually talking about protests of ethnic Serbs because of the abrupt changes in the make-up of the police force?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I'm saying. That's not what I mean, that you think I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that tensions grew and that in Knin there was a rebellion and that the Serb rebels started to attack the police stations in Knin, Petrinja, Pakrac, and Daruvar. The police was the sole armed force of Croatia. And then you go on to say that in 1990, 85 per cent of the policemen were Serbs and there were 15 per cent of Croats. That means that they attacked themselves; is that right? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the national structure, the ethnic composition in the police station of Slatina, and this figure relates to that particular police station. As to the other police stations, the situation was similar. At the level of the ministry, this ratio was 65/70 -- or 70/30. That was the ratio, although the Serbs in Croatia were not a majority ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that the percentage that held true for the whole of Croatia or for the areas where the Serb population represented the majority. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in those areas, that ratio was even less favourable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You spoke yesterday about the attack launched on your own police station, whereas in fact you deny that yourself, because you say that the leaders of the SDS party, they weren't leaders, SDS leaders Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at all, they were just demonstrators who were demonstrating in front of the place station, asked the chief of the police station, Kresimir Libl, guarantees that the arms would not being taken out of the police station. Is that correct? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the reason or, rather, an alibi that was used because there were no intentions to take away the weapons and this kind -- and we didn't expect an attack like that. We managed to collect the necessary number of people to prevent the militant masses entering the police station building and taking control of it, because we knew what this meant, what it would mean when a police station was taken over such as the one in Knin, Pakrac, and the other places where the barricades had already been set up and where the Croatian authority was not functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it true, Mr. Matovina, that the protests that you were talking about were organised precisely out of fear that the HDZ would not arm itself by taking away these weapons from the police station? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. Who would officially give weapons to the HDZ, taking it from the police station? This was something that no -- it never entered anybody's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Matovina. Is it true that the only demands of the citizens being assembled was that weapons should not be taken out of the police station? Is it true that the amassment of the population was that they were afraid of the pogrom that threatened the Serb ethnic group and which in fact did take place later on against these people? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't because, at the last moment, they managed to prevent the militant masses from entering the police station and taking it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, these were demonstrations in front of the police station, not an attack on the station. You yourself say that there was a large mass of the people and had they intended to storm the police station and enter it, they would have done so, and that emerges from what you yourself said.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would not have entered because it was the only police station which was attacked and defended successfully. The other ones which were attacked at that time were taken over, and after the police stations were taken over, it was evident how power and authority functioned in them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Matovina. You said yourself that the people were armed, that there were many people there - of course, you didn't see the weapons yourself - and that nobody on that occasion was injured, neither did anybody shoot at anybody else. So there was, in fact, no attack. Isn't that right, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that on that occasion, Mesaros Mato's car was overturned. The man was carved up himself but his life was saved through the efforts of the few of us that came to his aid. I also said that the militant masses did shoot and that after the mass dispelled, there was several hundred shells in front of the police station from the bullets that had been fired, several hundred casings. Therefore, the mass of people gathered in front of the station were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Whether the masses were armed or not, and let's not go into the casings that you're talking about, I really don't know anything about those events, all I do know is what you said and that it emerges from that that nobody was injured. And that particular citizen that you mentioned turned his car into the masses although he could have taken a roundabout road which would have been faster. He entered the masses purposely, and there are many witnesses to that, and on the occasion, he injured many people. Do you remember that, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did drive through the mobs, and as I said yesterday, his aim was to reach the health centre as quickly as possible, which is where his ailing wife was lying. And it was unusual, at least up until that time, that such a large mass of people in an unorganised fashion, without any security, should be found on the main road, gathered on the main road, blocking the communications there and paralysing communication in town generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Matovina, as you know your town very well - I've never been to that town - some of the people from the town who took part in this event said that it was much faster for him to use other byroads to get to the hospital rather than drive into the mass of population that he drove into, injuring more than ten people. Do you remember that, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not injure anybody. He didn't drive into the masses at any great speed, the speed that you're talking about now, and nobody asked for medical assistance. Now, why he didn't take a byroad, I really can't say, a roundabout way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, have you ever heard of somebody driving into the masses rallying at a rally?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all kinds of things happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not discuss that topic any further. Do you remember the decision to block all the barracks, the JNA barracks, in Croatia by a uniform decision taken by the command? That was taken in the second half of August, 1991. And the decision to attack all the units of the JNA from the 14th of September, 1991. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spoke about that yesterday, and I think the decision that you are talking about now refers to the so-called gentlemen's agreement that was reached when the government of the Republic of Croatia made an agreement with the JNA on the peaceful leaving of the infrastructure and localities where its units had been put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, for example, that of these events in Split on the 6th of May up until the 25th of July in Croatia, 126 cases were recorded of attacks on the members of the JNA and the JNA facilities, and all they were to blame for was that they were stationed in Croatia on the Croatian part of Yugoslav territory as members of the JNA. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as that particular fact and figure is concerned, I don't know anything about that, but I do know that there was a burgeoning distrust in Croatia towards the JNA. The people were ill disposed towards it because they saw that it was not what it purported to be. It was not a Yugoslav army, neither was it a Yugoslav People's Army. And it is in the events that took place that it took one side against another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The previous witness said here that the JNA, where it appeared, separated the two belligerent parties, the two conflicting parties, and that it did not take sides, but let's leave that for the time being for somebody else to talk about. Do you remember this: On the 31st of October, 1991, 15 villages were cleared in the Grubisno Polje municipality? Do you remember that? Fifteen Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I said that throughout that time I was in Slatina. Now, what happened in other areas, I really can't say. Don't ask me about that because I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you spoke here about other regions too, but do you remember on the 13th of December, 1991, the 13th of December, 1991, I say, when over 100 settlements in the Podravska Slatina municipalities - Daruvar, Orahovac, Slavonska Pozega - were cleansed and the Serbs expelled on the 13th of December, 1991. That's when that took place. I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Yes, Mr. Matovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know about that piece of information. I said yesterday that on that occasion, the paramilitary units withdrew and so did part of the population from the areas that I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if there had been -- you were in Slatina, and you were the police chief there. If 100 settlements in the municipality had been cleansed, you would have known about that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Slatina at the time, and I was the assistant chief of the police station, whereas Mr. Milosevic, in his question, asked about whether I knew about the Pozega, Daruvar, Orahovica and Slatina municipalities. The part that I testified to, which was from the Slatina municipality area where I was the assistant to the chief of police there, I can say that yes, it is true that the population did withdraw with the paramilitary units up until the line -- the Pozega-Kamensko-Pakrac line towards the later established UNPA zone. And as for the settlements of Pozega and Daruvar and the rest, I really don't know what Mr. Milosevic is asking me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. Just deal, if you would, with the area that you know about, which is Slatina. You say that the population or some of the population withdrew. Was there -- the question was: Was there any cleansing of that population? That is, was the population forced out? The Serb population, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb population was not forced to leave by the Croatian authorities. It went voluntarily with a portion of the rebellious Serbs and the units which were stationed there or set up -- rather, set up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that they themselves voluntarily left hundreds of settlements on the territory of these municipalities. That's what you're saying, Mr. Matovina. Now, tell me this: As you yourself said that on the 14th of December, the Croatian army took over control over that whole territory, according to your knowledge and information, how long did the fighting go on to take control of the territory and to expel the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Serbian population was not expelled at all. On the 14th of December, what happened was that after the withdrawal and after the order, the units of the paramilitary and the fact that the population went with it, the Croatian authorities took control of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You at least agree with the dates that I quoted. The 13th of December, 1991, that was the date I say that 100 settlements were emptied. You're talking about Slatina alone. Tell me, please, why in all this fighting and taking control of the area, it was precisely on the 13th - control had already been assumed by the Croatian army on the 14th [as interpreted] - why, then, you made the exception of Vocin? Why did you exempt Vocin when a hundred settlements were emptied and when you yourself say that these people who, according to your claims, were killed and fell victim, that they fell victim not only in Vocin but in other settlements as well? Why did you set aside Vocin from these hundreds of settlements?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday I spoke about an area which came under the composition of the former municipality of Slatina and the localities in which the crimes were committed when the paramilitary units withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, Mr. Matovina: What does Serbia have to do, and even the JNA -- and Serbia was not in command of the JNA -- what did it have to do with those events, for example, in Vocin that you took to be an example?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you asking me this? You know yourself what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't worry about why he's asking it. Did you see any involvement of the JNA or any Serbian involvement in what happened in Slatina? Can you help us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that the overall arming of the rebel units was organised by the JNA and that preparations were carried out on the part of the commanding officers, that mobilisation had taken place and additional training as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, even in this criminal report that you presented yesterday - and I've just had a chance to glance through it, but that was sufficient for me to form an opinion, everybody, literally everybody, without exception, against whom you filed a criminal report were exclusively your own citizens, citizens from that area. I don't assume that that is being challenged because that is what it says in the criminal report itself. And then after that, further on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with these things one at a time. Let's get the report. I take it that the report being referred to -- Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you can help us. It's presumably the report that was referred to by the Prosecution which names a number of suspects, which is tab 5 of Exhibit 334.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's actually the crime charge brought to the district public prosecutor in Osijek, and it refers to Cetekovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Matovina, what is being put to you is that the suspects that are referred to there are -- all have -- let me see what it is. Were all citizens of your area and not, therefore, Serbs from Serbia. Just a moment. Let the witness deal with the point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that all the people against whom criminal reports were filed and who were said to be guilty of the massacre in Cetekovac, in the area of Slatina, were people who had been mobilised into paramilitary formations. They had been armed with JNA weapons, and they were even dressed in JNA uniforms, the type of uniforms used by the reserve force. We have eyewitness statements about that. As for the other part of the list indicating members of the so-called White Eagles people or, rather, men who had come from Serbia that we had discussed yesterday, I can say there were no criminal reports against them because all we had were their full names and no other details. At that time, there was no communication with Serbia, so it was never possible to establish the identity of these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But look further on. What you said is all right, because it says here in black and white that these are local citizens from your area. But in the same report, you say Description of Facts: They wrote out 50 symbols of four-S slogans. "Everything is Serbian," then "Vuk Draskovic," "We will kill Tudjman," and again "Vuk Draskovic." What on earth has Serbia got to do with it, can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were the slogans that were put up on the facades of many buildings on the 31st of May, 1990, and in a number of villages Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. where, on the eve of the establishment of the SDS, this propaganda was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Matovina. So out of 100 settlements that on the 13th December 1991 were evacuated, you found only one, Vocin. And here you say the Serbs had committed a massacre, while you remember very well that there was an explosion in Vocin. A warehouse of explosives and ammunition was blown up. I don't know even where these explosives and ammunition had come from, but it is a fact that everything was destroyed in the area around the warehouse and some people were injured.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that explosion. All I know is that Vocin and the surrounding villages were completely destroyed during their retreat. What explosion are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The explosion that we have data about. And you mentioned it yesterday. You said only one place in Vocin was blown up. It was actually a warehouse of explosives and ammunition, and nobody was able to establish the cause.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Explosives were sent to that building and there was a stock of explosives and ammunition, while the surrounding houses were torched and blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was a building that was used as a storage place for explosives and ammunition and that's how it came about?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was blown up precisely on the day of the retreat and the massacre that happened that night in Vocin between the 12th and the 13th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But do you realise, Mr. Matovina, since you said it yourself, on the 14th of December the Croatian army took over all these areas, do you realise it was all that happened in this fighting between you in those local conflicts on that entire territory during the offensive of the Croatian army? Because said it yourself. This happened on the 13th, and on the 14th the Croatian army took over the entire area. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the times don't coincide. They speak against you. The 13th was the eve of the day of the Croatian takeover.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me assist in clarifying this case. On the case -- in the case file, we even have a criminal report filed by the prosecutor's office of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka against several persons who had blown up the Virgin Mary church in Vocin, and they qualified it as damage to property of others. However, in some witness statements, we have indications that completely different people did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into who did it and what it was about. I want you to explain, because you know it, unlike me who can only now gather information, that it was all about a Croatian offensive, an offensive of the Croatian army resulting in a conflict between the local Serb population and the Croatian authorities. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I made it clear yesterday and earlier today how these events occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, as a policeman, about the events in the area of Pakrac, the Pakrac field and the mass liquidation of Serbs in Marino village and Pakrac field on the 9th of October, 1991, when several smaller death camps were established, including Ribarska Koliba in Marino Selo and another one in Pakrac field. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never visited Pakrac. I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, do you remember -- have you heard anything about this: From 11th October to 29th March, 1992 -- 11th October 1991 to 29 March 1992, in your area several hundred Serbs were liquidated from about a hundred settlements, and these were villages, with the exception of the Pakrac area, in a location which was not actually involved in any armed conflict. These places were outside the area of armed conflict. You said yesterday when I told you about this and enumerated some villages, you said there was no conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Now, what is the question? Mr. Matovina, what has been put, you've dealt with the hundred settlements. We're not going back to that. But what is being put is between the 11th of October, 1991, and the 29th of March, 1992, in your area, it's said, several hundred Serbs were liquidated. Now, can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That is not correct, and I know nothing about it. For every event that we knew about, and I spoke about this yesterday, in individual cases we reacted according to legal procedure, from identifying eyewitnesses to finding perpetrators, and I -- as far as what this gentleman is talking about, I really know nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about the broader area of Western Slavonia, since there there was no one to protect them? Tens of thousands of Serbs on horse-drawn carriages left the area of Pakrac, Slatina, and other places where they were the majority population.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I wasn't there at the time, and you probably mean the events when the population and the army or, rather, members of the paramilitary formations were withdrawing from that area, but I wasn't there and I can't talk about it. I wasn't there in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that from June 1991 to August 1992; 193 settlements were completely cleansed, 183 urban and -- 183 villages and ten towns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've put your case. You've been told before that merely making allegations against the other side is not necessarily a defence. Now, have you got any cross-examination about his evidence or the documents he produced?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these questions are about his testimony, and I would like to remind you, Mr. May, that the previous witness, since he didn't agree with me about the figure that I had about 183 villages, he said it wasn't 183, it was 165. As if 165 was a lesser crime even if it were true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, you heard about Bljesak, the Flash operation. How many Serbs were killed during those 36 hours? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't because I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Western Slavonia at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Flash was an operation of the Croatian army involving a blockade of the Lipovac-Zagreb road. And after talks and negotiations, when they failed to find a way out of it and an agreement, they proceeded to block the road in the entire area. But further on from Slatina is an area where I didn't go. I did not participate in Operation Flash, and I can't talk about how the operation was carried out and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it is not disputable that it happened in Western Slavonia where you hail from. You're telling us that you know nothing about it? You worked there, after all?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a generally known fact that Croatian authorities eventually deblocked the area. I'm not denying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know how many people were killed then and how many thousands of houses were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I did not take part in Operation Flash. I was in Slatina all the time. I don't know how the operation was carried through, and I certainly can't testify to the details you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that in the beginning of 1991, the leadership of the then SFRY, that is Yugoslavia, attempted to arbitrate in the resolution of the conflict between Knin and Zagreb but all their attempts failed because Croatia kept increasingly arming itself, increasing the police force and the National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is: Can you assist at all in your capacity in Slatina as to any attempts of the SFRY leadership to resolve, arbitrate in the issue? Can you assist about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from this perspective, I can say what I found out eventually as a regular citizen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You're just talking about your general knowledge as a citizen of the area; is that right? Mr. Milosevic, no point just asking general citizens about what they know or what they've read. We can hear evidence from the participants and we will look at the documents in due course. Now, move on to another topic with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not talk about the leadership of the state. Here is something specific: Do you remember an event in Borovo Selo when Serbs had accepted to remove roadblocks, to return the situation back to normal, and at the agreed time the police entered the village with two buses, two field vehicles and one passenger vehicle, contrary to agreement, all these vehicles full of policemen. And instead of talking to the population, they got out of their cars and started shooting all over the village. Do you remember that event? Do you remember that crime, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer. Do you know anything about this particular event, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember. I wasn't there, but I remember reading in the press, and the coverage was wide. A crime was committed against Croatian policemen who had entered that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, this is something you read in the papers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. That's all I know as a general citizen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, as a citizen, do you know that according to the census from 1981, and that was the last census whose information is completely accessible to the public, in the municipalities of Grubisno Polje, Gradiska, Novska, Orahovica, Pakrac, Slatina, which is your municipality, Slavonska Pozega, Virovitica, there were 251 settlements with an absolute overwhelming Serb majority and 32 settlements with a relative majority of Serbs. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as migration processes and ethnic make-up is concerned in Slatina, at least I spoke about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know, then, that in 1990 and 1991 and 1992, all of these were ethnically cleansed? You probably don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been through all this. Now, unless you've got something new to ask the witness, we'll bring this to a close. We're not wasting our time any more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have half an hour left, Mr. May, and that's the time you gave me yesterday. Not exactly generously, but I do intend to avail myself of that half hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't waste it by constant repetition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not really notice that I was repeating anything, but perhaps you know better about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 4, paragraph 6, you mention that the citizens who were gathered there, you call them rebels, and they were shouting slogans: "We are not giving our police. Long live Yugoslavia. This is our police." In your statement, you actually confirm that your fellow citizens, Serb fellow citizens, declared themselves in favour of Yugoslavia. So this part of your statement means that they did not want the HDZ to take their weapons away and to arm their own membership. Is that finally clear, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the chanting of the citizens who had assembled around the police station accurately. I said how the militant masses felt, the militant masses who were trying to break in. And I referred to all the details of this gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct what you say on page 5, paragraph 2, that there was no reaction from JNA barracks or, rather, that the JNA did not want to be on anybody's side or to interfere?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. That time, the JNA did not react.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talk about some documents that were found in barracks, et cetera. Is it correct that you personally did not find a single document from among those that you've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not find a single document, but when the barracks were put under the control of the Croatian army, documents were found in them, and these documents clearly showed that Serb reservists were called up and what specialties they had. I already said that I personally did not work on this case. It was 20 or so officials who were involved. I was the one who rounded off the file, so I did not carry out all the investigations together by myself. We worked together. As for all these materials that are compiled, somewhere this particular document can be found as well, that reservists were called up, that they were trained in barracks, and that they were issued weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, what you are saying just now, is that actually a description of the regular reception of reservists which went the same way for decades? They were called up to barracks, they had military training exercises; of course they would get weapons for these military training exercises, and that is the only activity that you really describe. That's the way it was in 1980, in 1970, in 1960 and when you did your military service. How else are reservists trained anyway?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it was before. However, that time, after the training was completed and after the weapons were received, the reservists did not return to their homes. They went to areas that later came out of the control of the Croatian authorities and the illegal units were already being established in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you explain a few minutes ago that these reservists or territorials, as you called them in different ways, that they left the area together with their families? That is to say that they returned to their families, and they left the area together with their families under the pressure of the attacks of the Croatian army that took control on the 14th of December, according to what you said? Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about mobilisation when it was in full swing, and I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. talked about what was going on at the military barracks when the training started and the mobilisation started. That is March, April. And it became even more intensive in May and June. I spoke about the chronology of these events, and I also described how the armed insurgency throughout Croatia was developing, and then it was reflected on the area that I have been talking about too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 23rd of January, 1991, when the federal Secretariat of National Defence was saying the exact contrary, that using as a pretext an alleged military intervention - and there was no military intervention, especially not against Croatia - that intensive pressures were organised against the members and units of the JNA, also that certain facilities were guarded by persons with arms, there were terrorist attacks that were launched against the army and its soldiers, and that the army then said if Croatia does not disband these armed units, it will act in accordance with the decisions of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, and it will raise combat readiness to a level that will guarantee the implementation of the Law on Criminal Procedure, that is to say carrying out this in accordance with that law? There was a legally provided procedure. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as a citizen, I can say to you that the JNA was resolute in its demands and that it did not respect the rights of peoples in the former Yugoslavia, that they should be self-reliant or, rather, that the republics would have the right to become independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Matovina, since in your statement you say that the Croatian guard was established only in October 1991 - you say that on page 6, paragraph 2 of your statement - do you know that that is not true, that these so-called ZNGs were promulgated on the 28th of May 1991? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps in other places, in other locations, but in Slatina at that time, a brigade of the Croatian army was officially established in the month of October. There wasn't any Croatian army there then. There was perhaps just a unit of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mention here that on the 4th of August, the army opened fire at the police station. You mentioned that on page 7 of your statement. You say, further on, that the officers of the JNA several days later visited the police station in order to see what actually happened, and they said to you then that they were shooting because they thought that the MUP would attack the barracks. However, that was a single incident, and they came to visit you on that occasion to express their regrets because they did not intend to intervene vis-a-vis you in any way. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that not a few days later but that they came on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The following day.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the following day. They came to see what actually happened. However, in terms of the intensity of the attack against the police station, in terms of the particular parts of the building that were targeted and the timing of the actual attack, the intentions of the JNA were quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We explained that yesterday all right. You say that you -- that you saw from a 50-minute -- from a 50-metre distance they could not see whether there were any policemen inside. You said it was night-time and they could not see at a 50-metre distance whether there were any policemen inside, but you say that you took the barracks on the 16th of December. How can you explain that Commander Babic of the barracks was sent to Bjelovar as a prisoner of war when you say there was no fighting involved, that one man came later to collect the pistol that he had forgotten previously? How come that the commander of the barracks was taken as a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Babic was not a prisoner of war. In spite of fact that the JNA opened fire at the police station, he was never held accountable. He personally asked that he and two other officers be driven away to Bjelovar where buses were ready and when -- where they were taken in and all these people were released on the same day. The conscripts, the soldiers, were released immediately and they went home. So nothing happened. What I've been trying to say is that on the next day, an officer came and he was quite free to look for his pistol and that this event speaks of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Matovina. You said just now that the soldiers went to their homes, and a little while ago you said that the soldiers took weapons and joined some rebels, insurgents. What is true out of the two?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to explain. These were soldiers who were conscripts, who were doing their regular military service. They went home to their parents all over Croatia or Yugoslavia, whereas in the other case I was referring to the reservists from the area of Slatina who were mobilised, trained, and armed by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that members of the Croatian MUP and the ZNG already on the 21st of September massacred 13 soldiers of the JNA in Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about that as a citizen. Again, I read about this in the papers, what happened, et cetera. I don't know about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many hundreds of attacks were launched against the JNA after the agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, we're going to deal with what this witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are giving evidence about what happened in Cetekovac on the 4th of September, 1991, but you were not in the village when that event occurred; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not there but I explained yesterday. I explained the entire chronology of the events involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But that's a different matter altogether. So you were not an eyewitness of a single thing that happened then.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an eyewitness of the event that took place right that very moment, but as for the rest --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I'm asking you whether you were an eyewitness. You were not an eyewitness. You did not see who killed 22 men whose bodies were found on the 5th of September. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that but I did speak to witnesses who came from the actual site, and I spoke to them during the first few hours after they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 9 of paragraph 4, you say -- you say, "I think --" "I think that the attack was carried out by special units because it was led by Boro Lukic. He was a reserve captain in the special sabotage unit of the JNA." Is that correct that this is only your assumption who carried out the attack and who killed these people? You don't really know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special platoon carried out this attack. There is testimony about this, even coming from some of the members of that actual platoon who were later interviewed by the police or, rather, who were accessible to police inspectors and to persons who were investigating the case, because the case was not completed on that day, it went on for several years, depending on when witnesses were available. And this had to do with the persons who took part in the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 8, paragraph 3, you say that the archives of the paramilitary forces, as you say, were found in Zvecevo, that a military plan of the attack on the village of Cetekovac were found. Were you present when these archives were found? Did you see a single one of these documents? Can you give a more detailed explanation as to who the persons who saw this plan were?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents were found by members of the Croatian army, and almost all of these documents, a large number of these documents were handed over to the police. They are being kept in the police still. I personally saw these documents. Part of the documents were copied and are attached to these files here. And I personally saw the plan of the attack on Cetekovac which was planned in accordance with all military rules. That is to say, the main thrust of the attack, the operations coming from the flanks, and everything else, just the military usually does this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now that you've been referring these documents, have you actually been speaking about the list of documents that we established were made by the Croatian police and also some lists where there is a stamp of the Croatian police on them? Are those the documents that you're referring to now?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday that the document that you were showing was just an accompanying letter which gives a list of the documents that are being provided and that the stamp of the Croatian police was affixed to these documents because these are photocopies. Originals are being kept in the police administration, or, rather, the police station in Slatina, and this stamp confirms that the copy is faithful to the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, on the photocopy that was given to us yesterday, even the stamp is a photocopy. It's not that the stamp is there to affirm that it is authentic, that it is equal to the original.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, because all of this was photocopied into -- in several copies; perhaps dozens of copies, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about the Papuk detachment, and you pointed out that this Papuk detachment followed the traditions of the 12th Slavonian Brigade which fought in the Second World War. Those were your words yesterday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a statement of several members of the unit that took part in the armed rebellion who were members of that unit, that detachment. Their testimony was that the detachment was established in order to follow these traditions with a view to liberating these areas. I don't know from whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you say that they followed the traditions of the 12th Slavonian Brigade that fought in the Second World War. I wrote down your exact words. Against who did this 12th Slavonian Brigade fight in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th Slavonian Brigade was a partisan brigade. It fought against the fascists in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it fought against the Germans and Ustashas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In relation to what you said, namely that you personally did not see anything and that you were not present, on page 9 of your statement, you say: "Sixty soldiers entered the village with artillery support, and at least 160 soldiers surrounded the village." On the basis of which facts and figures are you presenting the number of soldiers involved, and how do you describe all of this that you mention in your statement and only a short while ago you said that you personally did not see any of this?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this information is based on the statements of witnesses who survived this event. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of claims made by persons who were on the spot or on the basis of claims made by persons who had heard what had happened.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of a small number of persons who managed to hide and survive or, rather, flee from the village. Ten or more watched the incident with their very own eyes, because they were -- they could not be noticed, and they were even supposed to come and testify here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You think that the intention of the attack was to expel the Croats from that area. Tell me, then, why did the Croats not leave when the attack was so successful and so brutal?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about the consequences of the attack and what happened and what was supposed to happen. As for what was supposed to happen, I really don't know. My descriptions show quite evidently what the intention underlying the attack was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you, because the intention was, as you had put it, that the Croats should leave. Why did they not leave? You said the intention was for the Croats to leave. So the intention was carried out, the attack was carried out brutally, it was over. Why did they not move out if that was the intention, for them to move out?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only natural that later, after this attack against the village, this village remained on the front line and the members of the Croatian police and the National Guard Corps were sent there. And they prevented further attacks against this village and attacks against the villages facing the Podravina highway. That was the ultimate objective, to take that and to cut off the only road that led to Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Matovina. Let me draw your attention to page 9, the one but last paragraph of your statement, and I want to ask you: Is it true that the results of the investigation established that the events which you describe in Cetekovac, that in those events it was neighbours who took part, the neighbours and even relatives of the victims themselves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The reservists who were mobilised, armed, and trained, wearing the JNA uniforms of the reserve cadres from the villages of Balenac and Cojlug, some of them were recognised by family members of the casualties at the funeral in Cetekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, as I assume you were a reservist yourself of some sort, and if you weren't I'm sure you will know, that at least ten, 15, or perhaps 20 years prior to that that the reservists had, should they be called up to military exercises and mobilisation, they had their uniforms with them at home, the uniforms of the reserve forces which they obtained from their units in the JNA. Is that something you know about?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true that they had part of the equipment, that is to say uniforms and other equipment, but they never had weapons at all. They weren't allowed to keep those, nor the other type of equipment that is necessary for warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see anybody distribute weapons to them? From the JNA to these people who, as you say, set up paramilitary units. The army issued strict orders that paramilitary units should not be allowed to form, and if they were formed, that they should be disarmed. So do you have any personal insight into anything that you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the departure of the convoy, over 40 trucks carrying military equipment from the barracks in Nasice to the insurgent area and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the distribution of those weapons. I said that yesterday. And I spoke about the killing of a citizen of Serb ethnicity - his surname was Kokic - at the funeral in Ceralije, who didn't want to take up arms. And later on and at that time the Croatian police went out to investigate and later on it was seen that he was the one who refused to take up arms and was going to Slatina to report the whole case, however, he was killed on his way to Slatina. So those are the facts and figures relating to the distribution of weapons and the participation therein of the JNA and the arming of the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that weapons were distributed to them?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several witnesses, people later who came to the area and went back to Slatina and said during that night, after the arrival of the convoy, there was a massive distribution of weapons that took place. And up until that time, part of the weapons had already been brought into the area and distribution had already taken place, and the commanding officers had received this equipment from the training sessions in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the concrete specific events and what did Serbia have to do with them. Now I'm asking you about your entire testimony and all the events that you mentioned during your testimony. What on earth has the Republic of Serbia to do with any of these events that you are testifying about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will be a matter for us to determine. You've asked the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm asking him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've asked the witness once and he's given his answer. He identified people there from Serbia, he said. Now, have the amicus got any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. Very well. We will adjourn. We will take the break now. Re-examination afterwards and then we'll hear the next witness. Could you be back, please, in -- I think we have half an hour today. Twenty-five past, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, I'm going to ask you some questions now about a part of your evidence concerning the 14th of December, 1991, when you said the Serbs left voluntarily from your area of Slatina.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By that, did you mean the Serb civilian population?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb civilian population, yes, and the armed units which left the area together with them. Actually, they were forcing them to go with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's about the Serb civilian population that I wanted to ask you questions. By that, do you mean women, children, families were leaving their homes?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those who were in the area under temporary occupation. The rest of the Serbs who were where the Croatian authorities were, for the most part remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So those Serbs, as you say, under temporary occupation, do you mean by Serb rebel units? What do you mean by "temporary occupation"?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under the temporary control of the Serb rebel units which at that time controlled the area and where the Croatian authorities were not functioning. That is to say, not a single institution was in the hands of the Croatian state, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So in which direction did those people go, the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that they went in the direction of Pakrac where, later on -- which was to become the UNPA zone later on from the Pozega-Pakrac road right up to Okucani and towards Bosnia. And another portion went to Bosnia straight away, as far as my information tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what numbers are we talking about? Have you had any access to figures that you can help us with the amount of people of the civilian population who were leaving?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what numbers or figures they were from the village, but the majority left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to go now to the documents. I'm going to look at Exhibit 327 and tab 13 and go to attachments 57 and 58 where we looked at documents with the signature or name Munja, and you gave evidence about a man called Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if they could be put in front of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a list of the members of the Zvecevo detachment, with their first and last names, their ranks, their military registration number, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. We don't need to look at that. I'm looking at the documents in attachment 57, the first one with the name -- signature Munja and the stamp, and that's the document dated 14th of November, 1991. You've got it there in front of you. It's got "57" in the top right-hand corner. Just looking at this name Munja, you referred to another document where you said someone had written in hand that he had a name Vukelic. First of all, did you take part in the investigation of this particular matter concerning these documents?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, about 20 of the employees took part, and they looked at the archives of the paramilitary units from Zvecevo and studied them carefully, and they introduced a system into them. They systematised them as evidence and contribution and attachments to the reports for the Prosecution. And from speaking to the witnesses or, rather, individual members of the units that we're talking about, we learnt that behind the nickname Munja was the person of the man Veljko Vukelic, in fact, and one of the staff wrote this down on the first page that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The translation came to me that you used the word "we." I'm asking actually about you personally, whether this was a matter of the investigation that you were concerned with and knew about.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was one of them, one of the people who participated in the investigation, and I did know about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at that document there dated the 14th of November, 1991, where Munja's signature is, there is a stamp. Can you tell us what that stamp is?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to see, it says "The SAO Krajina, Slavonska Pozega," and the rest of it, the rest of the wording on the stamp are not readily legible. I think it says "The socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, Western" -- I can't really read what it says on this other part. It's a question of the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it an official stamp that you recognise or know about?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that stamp was the official stamp used in the area which was under temporary occupation, and it is still -- it can be found on a series of other documents too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's go to the document, then, in attachment -- at the end of the -- excuse me -- in attachment 58, which is dated the 5th of November, 1991, which has the handwriting, "Vukelic is the one hiding behind Munja." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to Vukelic, have you had any connection with this man? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know him while he was in Slatina holding the post before the war of the secretary of the committee, and later on, he was head of the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that he had close ties with the JNA, and you accused him of cooperating and distributing weapons to Serbs. Where does that information come from? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't accuse him of distributing weapons. What I was saying was that there was cooperation with the JNA and the Secretariat or Department for National Defence. I said that this cooperation or collaboration was close, that it was on a daily basis, and that it was the task of the department to call up the reservists and young men to do their military service, to engage in training, to compile military records and all the rest of the business of the defence department in connection with civilians. And I also said that in the first days of the uprising, he left the area and crossed over to the area which was later under the control of the rebel Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So as far as distribution of weapons is concerned, you're not saying anything against him in relation to arming the local population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite resolute in stating who armed the population and how the distribution of weapons was carried out. Now, which posts and offices he held later in the insurgent area, I don't know. I wasn't there. But from the documents -- from certain documents, we can see that he was in the top military and civilian echelons, or, rather, political structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to go on to one other matter now and that deals with the 4th of August, 1991, when you described the police station at Slatina as having been attacked by the JNA. That event took place at 2300 hours and about or near the time when there is a change of duty for the police. The record we have on the LiveNote translation is that the JNA was 50 kilometres away. I don't know whether that's right or wrong, because another figure has also been mentioned. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 50 metres, not 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all I need ask about that. Just the last matter I'm going to deal with is Exhibit 334, looking at tab tabs 6, 7, 8. These are three medical reports that you produced as part of your files of investigation. Tab 6 contains details of a person with some bruises and abrasions which have been noticed by the doctor on the body; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was a policeman by the name of Darko Bozickovic from Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
