utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Make it look like damage incurred in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to come back to that as a separate topic later, and shortly, but those events were known of. Did any political leaders - and if so, which ones? - go to the front, to your knowledge? And if so, what was their revealed attitude to the soldiers who they found there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Branko Kostic frequently went to that theatre of war, and we could see television footage of his visits. I didn't go even when he went there. And Branko Kostic and others went to inspect the troops. Television pictures and photographs showed them inspecting the troops and encouraging the soldiers. It was broadly covered by the press, both opposition and official press. You could often see Bulatovic and Kostic in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Seselj, did he feature at all at this time in any way in the campaign?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, a lot and very badly. Seselj played the part at that time of the Chetnik Vojvoda or Chetnik duke, and he got the title from a war criminal, Vojvoda Djuic who emigrated after the previous war. And in that capacity as a self-styled Chetnik duke, he inspected the troops who wore all the symbols of Chetniks from the previous war. I must say that it was a disgrace that such a glorious and chivalrous army should be inspected by a man like Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we stick, please, to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move from this general topic about the campaign Dubrovnik, I want to turn to somebody who had a party political importance, Bozidar Vucurevic, mayor of Trebinje. Did he have a political position at that time? And if so, in which party?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: That mayor is a former truck driver from Trebinje. He is in fact a village charlatan who became a big cheese at that time. He organised paramilitary units from Eastern Herzegovina to attack Dubrovnik, and he made jokes about the destruction of that town. His role is one of a great criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally - just yes or no to this first - did you hear anything of use of prisoners released from gaol fighting in this campaign? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I heard about that but I cannot confirm it because I didn't see it with my own eyes, but I have heard about such men being used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you say from whom you heard that? Can you say, according to the sources that you had, by whom they were released?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I heard this from my friends from Kotor and Budva and Titograd itself. But who actually released these men, I can't say. It is easy to conclude that they were released by their prison administration, if they were released at all. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We've dealt now with the 1st of October meeting. Let's move on from that meeting to the 4th of October and thereafter. Was there a meeting on the 4th of October?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a session of the government and a session of the parliament on the 4th and 7th of October respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you remember specifically what happened on the 4th as opposed to what happened on a later day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: We started with the initiative which was discussed on the 4th and the 7th of October, that our parliament should continue talks with the Croatian parliament. It was a matter for debate, difficult debate, because the differences in opinion were wide. There were extreme opinions that Croatia should not be talked to at all, but there were those who also thought that Montenegro should talk to Croatia and try to stop the war. This initiative was supported by President Bulatovic and Prime Minister Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you provided with reports on the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody sent any particular reports to me. We didn't receive any special reports. But it was so broadly discussed in the media, on television and in the press, that we knew at every moment exactly which line our troops had reached, which towns or areas they have control of and which they don't. It is likely that Bulatovic did receive some reports that I didn't, from generals, for instance, but we didn't even need any special reports because everyone knew --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: -- where Yugoslav units are, which towns they hold and which they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 338, tab 4. After the meeting of the 4th of October and before the meeting on the 7th, was this letter sent? While the original in Cyrillic goes on the overhead projector, I can explain that this is a letter from the government of the Republic of Serbia and the President Dragutin Zelenovic, dated the 5th of October. Now can we look at the English version, please. The text shows as follows -- or reads as follows: "The government of the Republic of Serbia, on its session held on October the 4th, have been acquainted with the danger to the civilian population and the city of Dubrovnik that represent a part of the Serbian and Croatian history, as well as a magnificent monument of the world cultural heritage. "Your decision to install paramilitary units, Black Legions, and numerous foreign mercenaries in a city of invaluable historical and cultural value, and to launch an armed attack on settlements in Herzegovina and Boka Kotorska from this position represents a totally uncivilised, inhuman, and undignified act." Boka Kotorska, of course, is the Bay of Kotor. "We help that you yourself are aware of this and that you will use all the forces at your disposal to stop destruction of Dubrovnik in order for it not to be destroyed, as other cities. "Addressing you with this letter to stop the destruction of Dubrovnik, the government of the Republic of Serbia expresses its firm conviction that all the members of the Yugoslavian army and troops of the Territorial Defence will put all the efforts to protect this historical town." Signed by President Dragutin Zelenovic and sent to the government of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb, or at least addressed there. Now, without becoming expansive about matters historical and trying to confine yourself, if you can, to the significance of this letter at that time and what it shows us about what was happening, your comment, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the 5th of October was the date on and around which war operations were carried around in Dubrovnik and around it. This is as cynical as anything that was done in the times of Goebbels. It says here that the Yugoslav army should defend Dubrovnik, the very army that was attacking it. You can't get any more cynical than that. It says here that the Yugoslav army is not taking part in this war; it is the Montenegrin troops which are involved. And this is written by a member the government of President Milosevic. And they are together in this. I must also say that the letter is also nonsensical. The Serbian Prime Minister knows precisely what the Territorial Defence of Montenegro and the Yugoslav army are supposed to do, although he personally isn't involved. This letter talks about things that I know very well about. I heard Minister Jovanovic say many times at the time that it is the Montenegrin army which is involved in the war, not the Yugoslav army. You can't get much more cynical than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 7th of October extraordinary session, can you tell us what was discussed then, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: It was similar like on the 4th of October. The Assembly passed a decision to negotiate with the Croats. And in the first sentence, it said - and this is very important and I really want to highlight it here - that the Assembly of Montenegro states that it recognises the will of the Croatian people, for them to have an independent state. I have to emphasise here that in spite of the war and in spite of all the troubles that prevailed then, Montenegro was the first one to recognise Croatia's independence along with Slovenia officially. So although this is contradictory to everything that was going on but that is a fact. This document does exist and you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, was anything else raised at this meeting that hadn't been particularly in issue before? And you remember we -- well, see if you can help us.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the context of what I was saying, namely that Montenegro accepts the independence of Croatia, and this was contrary to Slobodan Milosevic's policy which shows that the Montenegrin leaders did try to get out of his claws, was the fact that we started talking to Croatia. Dr. Adzic writes -- sorry, Dr. Kacic writes about this in detail in his latest book that was published in the English and Croatian languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can we move on, please, and stick to what the witness knew himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to see, in the next documents, reference to Prevlaka. It may be helpful, I think, at this stage if we use this map, which is going to be Exhibit 336, and it's just that little bit there. We can -- You're going to see, as I say, from documents shortly following that Prevlaka turned up. Was it discussed at this 7th of October meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's it. We took Prevlaka as a pretext to talk to the Croats in order to achieve some kind of peace to the extent of our possibilities, because you cannot really act against the army because the army holds everything in their hands. However, Prevlaka was taken as a pretext for us to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if the booth would be good enough to focus right down on the bottom right-hand corner of this map. If they can do that for us. No, literally. That's it. Perfect. Thank you. We can see on this map, Mr. Samardzic, the Prevlaka peninsula in green, and then we can see, in black, the border between Croatia and Montenegro leaving to the east a channel, I think that you would say was perfectly sufficient, for vessels to pass through and to remain in Montenegrin waters. Nevertheless, being overlooked by that peninsula that curves round and underneath the opening to the bay itself. In very short order, really just a sentence or so, what was the proposal that was put by you on behalf of the Montenegrins to Croatia about that boundary? Really, just in a sentence or so. The Judges haven't seen it before, and it will help them to have it in the most straightforward way possible. What was your proposal?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Our proposal was to rectify the border and for Prevlaka to belong to Montenegro. But this was a proposal that was put forth in friendly negotiations with Croatia, and also we wanted Croatia to accept this and we wanted to discuss Prevlaka on that basis. That is what it says in the document that we sent to the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the effect of that would have been to change the border that on this map has a pointy -- pointed top and then goes down, to change that to a line running presumably directly south or south-west. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: For the entire entrance into the Bay of Kotor to be Montenegrin, not to be shared with Croatia. This was our proposal, but on the basis of friendship with Croatia. That's what we said in the document, too. That's what we put in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit 338, tab 5, a number of documents. And on this occasion I shan't ask for them all to go on the overhead projector because I think it would be -- all the originals to go on the overhead projector because I think it would take too long. So hand the originals, please, to the witness, and just place the first page of the English version on the overhead projector. You see this coming to the Assembly of the Republic of Montenegro, October the 12th, to the speaker of the Croatian parliament, signed by Dr. Vukcevic, the president of the Montenegrin Assembly: "Dear Mr. Speaker, please find enclosed the initiative of the determination of the sea and land border between Montenegro and Croatia, by agreement put forth by the Assembly. We hope the Croatian parliament will accept our initiative and enter the negotiations." Copied to Lord Carrington and Hans Van den Broek. Next document, please. We'll try and deal with these fairly swiftly. The next document is in a couple of sheets and is the initiative itself, coming from -- described as Titograd, also Podgorica, on the 8th of October. The initiative, title set out, and it says this under paragraph 1, third line -- or perhaps better read all of it: "Taking into consideration the decision of the Republic of Croatia to become a sovereign and independent state, the Assembly of the Republic of Montenegro considers that such a decision, apart from raising a series of legal and state issues, also changes the status of the border between the Republic of Montenegro and the Republic of Croatia, as it has been to the present." Characterises it. Next paragraph, second line: "The existing border in the area of the Prevlaka peninsula is a hinderance to the establishment of a just and rational boundary in the coast waters and the continental shelf and therefore believes a minor correction necessary." Over the page, please. If the usher would be so good. Paragraph 3: "Montenegro has no interest in seeing further conflicts, destruction, and loss of human lives in the border area towards the republic. The population of those areas has lived in peace and mutual respect for centuries regardless of political systems. That is why this area is a tourist zone renowned throughout the world for the beauty of your Dubrovnik and our Bay of Kotor. "In an earnest effort to re-establish such relations as soon as possible, we address the Croatian parliament with an initiative to settle all pending issues, including the aforementioned issue of the land and sea border through dialogue and negotiations. If the Croatian parliament should accept this initiative, contact through Nikola Samardzic, MP, Minister of Foreign Affairs." Next document page, please. The history of the initiative is set out. The second paragraph: "The Assembly affirmed that the Republic of Montenegro is not at war with the Republic of Croatia, nor has it any territorial pretensions toward its territory. Reservists from Montenegro presently in the region of Dubrovnik and in Herzegovina are members of the JNA which is the only instance responsible for their deployment. We cannot, therefore, accept the standpoint of the Croatian parliament that Montenegro has performed aggression on the Republic of Croatia. On the contrary. Montenegro has and continues to promote peace, friendly and good neighbourly relations with Croatia." It deals with comments on tourism in the maritime economy. The next paragraph deals with the fact that the Bay of Kotor is actually so large that the coastline is 30 per cent of the entire coastline. Then it turns to the existing border and explains why the new border proposed would be a good one. The next sheet, please, of this document. And we see this set out, coming from Montenegro to Croatia: "One cannot deny the fact that these and similar circumstances aggravate the psychosis of war among a greater part of the Montenegrin population. They feel that Montenegro would be impaired and damaged if Prevlaka would belong to another state and if a foreign army base would be located there." Last paragraph: "The above makes it clear that Montenegro has no territorial pretensions but only wishes that an agreement be reached on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the establishment of lasting peace." Was the problem, or did the problem in any event include that Prevlaka was simply used as a military base, Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: You ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Just yes or no, probably.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents that you read out just now were ones written by me personally. They were approved by President Bulatovic and by Prime Minister Djukanovic. The objective was to start negotiations with the Croats and to stop the war. That was far more important than Prevlaka. Everything that is written here is true, and regrettably, it was in contradiction with the actual state of affairs because war was being waged in Dubrovnik and a march further on towards Karlobag was being planned. However, these are documents and this is what really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The Croats --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, we're going to look at the rest of the documents in this exhibit, but I just wanted to get a little detail in for the Judges. Was Prevlaka in fact used as a military installation and for nothing else? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a military base then, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fine. Let's --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: During the Second World War, it was a prison for the anti-fascists. This was during the Second World War. Otherwise, before the Second World War, during the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and later on during Tito's Yugoslavia, it was a military base.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next part of this exhibit, please, if the usher would be so good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the only substantial exhibit that is more than a single or a couple of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now come to Titograd, dateline the 8th of October, from the Assembly, conclusions of the session on the 7th of October: "The Assembly obliges the delegation of the Republic of Montenegro to insist on its further work on the principal orientation of the Republic of Montenegro that all disputes in Yugoslavia can and must be settled through political negotiations. The delegation of the Republic of Montenegro is obliged to insist the issue of the future arrangement of relations in Yugoslavia can be resolved in such a way as to guarantee and protect full and equal rights of all citizens, republics, and nationalities." Then paragraph 3: "Obliges the delegation to be open to any initiative which may lead to a just and principled resolution of the crisis." Perhaps you'd best look over the page to paragraph 5 where there's a further reference to a principled solution to the border issue, and then says: "The Assembly accepts in principle the fundamental principles for the arrangement of future relations in Yugoslavia as well as the related conclusions of the committee for constitutional matters of the Assembly of the Republic. The Assembly of the Republic considers these fundamental principles an initiative and sound basis for finding an optimal solution to the issue of future arrangement of relations." Perhaps you would look at the last couple of pages and we'll come back to your evidence on the topics. Finally, we have a document on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that document either. Until now, they were in this same order, no mean achievement as opposed to yesterday, but now I can't find it. I can't find this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see you get another one. Perhaps he could have another clip, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. If it's only the October the 15th document he's missing, I'm sure we can find one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This the reply then, sent on the 15th of October from the speaker of the Republic of Croatia coming to the President of the Assembly in Montenegro. Just read a few of the passages. Second paragraph on the first page. "I'm sure that the atmosphere for discussion and dialogue would have been more favourable had your initiative appeared before the aggression on the Republic of Croatia from the territory of Montenegro. This conclusions of October the 8th, the Croatian parliament did not declare the Republic of Montenegro the aggressor but rather the Republic of Serbia and the so-called JNA or what is left of it. Over the page, perhaps, without doing a disservice to the document, and at the top: "Your assertion in item 3 of the initiative that Montenegro has no interest in seeking further conflicts, destruction, and loss of human lives in the border area towards the Republic of Croatia raises a certain amount of hope that peace and good neighbourly relations can return --"

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can I have the document in Serbo-Croatian? No it's not that. It's not that. I have not also the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There appears to be a photocopying shortcoming. No, Your Honour, this one may not actually exist in B/C/S, in which case I hope we'll be permitted to continue with it in English, and I'll inquire into the status of any other translation as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you happy to follow it in English, Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we just go down the page from where we were, come towards the bottom, a short paragraph. "... especially concerned by your statement that there are certain circumstances which aggravate the psychosis of war." And then the last paragraph: "We therefore accept your proposal that direct contacts be established, and we invite your designee, Mr. Nikola Samardzic, MP," and so on, "to visit Zagreb as soon as possible without delay." Mr. Samardzic, just this on this little collection of materials of one kind or another: So far as you could judge, was the Montenegrin approach for a negotiated settlement including settlement of the little border issue genuine? And were you sincere?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was absolutely sincere. I made every effort I could, and I really wanted negotiations to be accepted, and I really wanted these negotiations to start and to have a ceasefire in this way, and also to put a stop to the aggression against Dubrovnik. I believe that Momir Bulatovic, also having seen where Slobodan Milosevic's policy would lead everyone to, I believe that he also supported this, because we discussed it often. This what I wrote on the Montenegrin side is something that he approved, and together we got a reply from Mr. Domljan, the speaker of the Croatian parliament, and I know that he was pleased that there were this favourable response and it was agreed that I would go to Zagreb. However, at the very last moment, this was stopped, and I imagine that it was stopped from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was any reason given for your visit being stopped?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: It was said officially, officially allegedly, that I could not travel to Zagreb because one had to travel to The Hague. This was written on the 15th, and then this came on the 17th, two days later, when we received Lord Carrington's proposal. And then I went to The Hague rather than to Zagreb. However, there were also words to the effect that I shouldn't go to Zagreb. "Don't go there. They'll kill you there," et cetera. However, I paid no attention to this because everything that was agreed upon was agreed upon verbally. Also with Dr. Kacic, because I was in constant communication with him. And the only purpose for this was for us to achieve some kind of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I turn on to the next couple of days of October this same year, can you just tell us, please, a little bit more about two things featured in the Dubrovnik campaign? Was there talk of something called the Dubrovnik Republic at about this time? If so, was it serious?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Of course there was talk about the Dubrovnik Republic. There was this major campaign that Dubrovnik should purportedly be liberated and become some kind of an independent Republic of Dubrovnik within a Greater Serbia, and they started working on this. This was done by the military circles, by the military, the counter-intelligence service. And the Montenegrin government did not take part in this. It was the people's party, a pro-Chetnik organisation that was formed during those days. They took part in it and they were absolutely involved in this with the army to create a Republic of Dubrovnik. And they held meetings in Cavtat. This could be seen on television. They also wrote about this in their newspapers. Individuals came to see me and to ask me whether this Dubrovnik Republic could be established. Everybody had reasons of their own why they put this question, and interests of their own, and as I said, this was discussed during those days. It was discussed rather extensively, this Dubrovnik Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it ever discussed or talked about between you and Jokic or Strugar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I know Jokic, because he was in the navy, and he often came when he was commander of the navy zone of Boka to see me at my office. Well, it wasn't that often, but he did come and that's how we knew each other. I did not know Strugar, though. I just saw him at the session that was held on the 1st of October. But what I want to say now is the following: During these war operations - I cannot remember the exact date, it was probably the end of October, beginning of November - when things were not going well for the Yugoslav army in Dubrovnik, three Englishmen came, officials of the European Union. I saw that they were citizens of the United Kingdom. And they asked me to establish contact for them with Admiral Strugar and Admiral Jokic. Somebody from the government had sent them to me although at that time I did not know where Strugar was and where Jokic was. I managed to find Strugar and Jokic through the Ministry of Interior of Montenegro, and I talked to Jokic. I said to him that these gentlemen were looking for him in order to negotiate with a view to establishing peace. They accepted that, and immediately after that, they started asking me whether it was possible to organise a Republic of Dubrovnik. That's what they asked me. Jokic asked me and Strugar also asked me, could I explain this to them, and that was on the telephone. They were at the front line and I was in my office in Titograd. I said to them forget about that completely. That is impossible. That's a bad thing. It's no good. And if you wish any good to your army and to your country, you should absolutely and totally forget about this. This is a chauvinist idea that is going to backfire against the Serb people the most. They did not make any comments, but that's what I said to them and I would like to confirm here that they were asking me from the front line as to whether a Republic of Dubrovnik could be established, because obviously they had their doubts. They saw that people around Dubrovnik would not hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you become aware at that time of any evidence to suggest that the citizens of Dubrovnik themselves wanted separation from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No way. Not a single person from Dubrovnik, a true person from Dubrovnik, at least these generations, never showed any intention of this kind to secede from Croatia. This is a pure lie, propaganda. The Republic of Dubrovnik ceased to exist in 1797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now we're going to come to the Carrington Plan, to the role of Jovic, Kostic, Bulatovic, yourself, and the accused in that plan, and to the visits here to The Hague. I think, Mr. Samardzic, it will be sensible for you to give, if you can, a concise narrative of events, including an account of your speech, a summary of your speech, please, which we can see in an exhibit in a minute, or at least some of it. And if you either go for too much detail or too little, you'll have to put up with my interrupting you, and I hope you don't mind. We've dealt with your planned visit in October and its cancellation. Just remind the Chamber of what Lord Carrington's plan was and then explain the Montenegrins' involvement in it, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: After holding a number of rounds of negotiation on the establishment of peace, quite obviously it became clear to the European Community that the warring parties in Yugoslavia were unable to agree amongst themselves, and Lord Carrington, who was the chairman of the peace conference on Yugoslavia on the 17th of October sent to all the republics, that is to say the presidents of all the republics, six of them, a plan on how to settle the crisis in Yugoslavia and to establish peace. In short, the plan contained the following: That the federal republics of Yugoslavia should become independent states and members of the United Nations. Furthermore, that they could associate and form an association of independent states if they wished to do so. They can associate -- form associations amongst themselves. A special status was established for national minorities and in the annex it was clearly stated that this related to the Serb minority in Croatia. Therefore, the inhabitants of the Serbian Krajina region, or the SAO as it was referred to then, the autonomous areas, were given rights like an independent state. They had their judiciary, their own police force, their own economy, their own educational system, their own tax system, everything section except the army. And the Croatian army along those lines was not supposed to be within that territory, that is to say the Serbian territory, but the international community. That is the gist of Lord Carrington's plan. At 6.00 on the 17th of October, that plan was presented and President Bulatovic had it copied and he convened a meeting of the Montenegrin parliament. It was only the Montenegrin parliament of all the other six republics that this was discussed and televised throughout Serbia, Bosnia and perhaps Macedonia, and parliament called for a decision to be taken as to whether Lord Carrington's plan was to be adopted or not. Now, you mentioned my own presentation on that particular evening. What I said was that Lord Carrington's plan must be adopted, and I emphasised the following: Unless we accept Lord Carrington's plan, we are leading the Serbian people in Croatia into the greatest possible abyss and they will come upon hard times. And I also emphasised that if we failed to adopt Lord Carrington's plan, the United Nations would enforce sanctions and a sanitaire cordon would be set up. I emphasised all that. I said that we could not win a war of this kind because the morale of our army and our people, as it was an unjust war, was running low, and a war Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of this kind could not be won. I also emphasised that when Britain went to war, then it was the son of the British monarch that was in the forefront, whereas our own leaders kept their sons at home in safe places or abroad whereas it was the poor people that went to war. So I put all that forward, I emphasised all that, and I almost got beaten up on that particular evening. I was called a traitor. Some ultra nationalistic people stormed the Assembly, and they really wanted to beat me up. But always I say, we in Montenegro waged this kind of discussion from 7 in the evening to 7 in the morning. And at 7.15, we left by special plane --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, it may be difficult but you're in a court and just answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, okay, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the passage so far, having spoken to the witness at some length --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- I judged it probably wise to let him give a summary because it would probably be quicker than the interruptions of questions and answers that I would have to make to elicit the same information. We've reached the position where we can put into evidence a summary of his speech because it's an exhibit. I've missed out Exhibit 6 and we will have to come back and deal with that. Perhaps I'll deal with that straight away. Then we can look at Exhibit 7 and that may be time for a break, that being a matter, of course, for the Court and not for me. Can we just look at Exhibit 6 because we then have it -- not Exhibit 6, tab 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go on to -- if it's all right with the interpreters, we'll go on until 4.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 6 of 338, just to get a little bit more context. This is a letter from Dr. Vukcevic of the 16th of October. Original, please, to the witness and English on the overhead projector. Of course the previous document was in English, not in B/C/S. It follows the normal plan where we have documents only in English they aren't translated into B/C/S. If they're in one or other of the languages of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, then. This document, just to deal with it: "Mr. President, we acknowledge the receipt of your letter..." Next paragraph but one -- it is the Assembly of Montenegro speaking: "Our influence on the JNA is rather limited. We are doing all we can in the area of Dubrovnik to try and help calm the situation down, help the beginning of at least a gradual withdrawal of JNA units. Our efforts with the army would be a great deal more effective if individual actions against its soldiers ceased. Each individual killing or wounding of a JNA soldier is making our efforts with the army and our attempt to reduce the war psychosis in the Republic more difficult. "We believe that the first results of our efforts are already apparent since the army representatives have agreed with the Dubrovnik authorities to repair the equipment for the supply of water and reconnect electricity. "We have interpreted the arrival of JNA units into Cavtat and Zvekovica as an agreement between the JNA and the representatives of Dubrovnik authorities with the mediation of the international observers. We will do everything we can to help the population of the Dubrovnik region... "Tomorrow ... the Assembly will sit in session, and the following day, 18 October, a peace conference will be held ... where the delegations will be led by the presidents of the republics." And then it states: "Nikola Samardzic, our parliamentary deputy ... is unable to come to Zagreb tomorrow or the day after due to these obligations." Is that the letter that sets out the reasons that were given to you for your non-attendance upon Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the reasons I was presented with, because we were to go to The Hague, and that's what it looked like. But quite obviously, I was not able to go to Zagreb. However, the Hague conference was far more important at that particular point in time. It was more important for me to accompany President Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, which is a record that you've made. You will have to give us a date of it. A record you've made in an English fax format, I think, or similar. Summary and shortened version of your speech. You've already given us an account of that, about not being traitors, accepting the peace proposal, Lord Carrington hasn't destroyed Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav leaders did that. We cannot win this war. Morale is low, reference to the rich families spending time on the beaches, reference to the English royal family, stop the violence, United Nations sanctions an alternative, must negotiate. When did you prepare -- just that's all I want to know, Mr. Samardzic. When did you prepare this summary of your speech? Very recently or at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: At that time. That is part of the text which I wrote when the Jugooceanija ships were blocked, they were stopped because of the sanctions, seven of them in the ports of the United States of America. And I prepared material for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need to know. The question was when you prepared the document. Let's now go on with the Carrington Plan. We'd reached the stage where, following the discussion, you were all due to come here to The Hague. How did you travel? Obviously, you flew here, but who did you travel with?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: With President Bulatovic and the security provided. We flew in a small plane directly from Titograd to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Bulatovic say anything about the negotiations of which he was to be a part?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. We went to The Hague to say yes or no vis-a-vis Lord Carrington's plan, and we held a parliamentary session throughout the night. He still wasn't quite sure and hadn't reached a decision in the plane, but he was quite sincere and said that Lord Carrington's plan was the only way out of the situation and the predicament that faced us. But he was afraid of President Milosevic, what he would do, and he didn't know himself what President Milosevic would do at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the meeting itself, did there come a chance for people to speak in order on the merits of the plan? If so, what was the order in which people were to speak?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The custom was that the representatives of the republics should present their views in alphabetical order, which meant that Bosnia was due to speak first and then Serbia in front of Slovenia. And this took place in the plenary session. However, may I just add that when we arrived in The Hague, we met Lord Carrington and he was worried and concerned whether Croatia would accept the plan. He didn't doubt that Serbia would, but he had quite a lot of disquiet as to whether Croatia would and whether President Tudjman would refuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When it came time to speak, who spoke first?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: President Milosevic took the floor first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His attitude toward the plan?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: His attitude was that he was very firm in rejecting the plan and said he did not agree with it and stated the following more or less: The Croats have the right to set up their own state, but if they have that right, so do the Serbs, to -- in Croatia to go to their state, the state of Serbia, or to Yugoslavia, and he said that is why he disagreed with the Carrington Plan, that the Serbs should stay in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what manner, with what moderation or otherwise was that view expressed by the accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. Yes. Just answer the question. What?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are documents, Mr. May. They all exist. Minutes exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. He can --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand why you're letting the witness recount what I myself said when you have records of that. It was all recorded at the international conference, word for word. So why hear his interpretation? I didn't talk to him privately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him give -- he can give -- he can give his evidence about it. If it's wrong, you can contradict it with the minutes when we produce them in due course, no doubt, if such exist. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can read through the minutes too. I don't see why I should listen to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, can you answer the question, please? What was the manner, the moderation or otherwise, of the accused at the time he took the floor and expressed the view he did?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question. He said that Croatia had the right to set up its independent state, but so did the Serbs in Croatia. They had the equal right of living in their own state, and that is why they cannot accept -- could not accept the plan devised by Lord Carrington. And he adamantly rejected it. And I agree with the president --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now come to the voting of the others and in particular the voting of Bulatovic and what happened then. Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: After the speech that was made by President Milosevic, everybody took the floor in alphabetical order, and they accepted Lord Carrington's plan in its entirety. The Croats were particularly pleased because they had no need to reject the plan now that President Milosevic had rejected it. Montenegro and President Bulatovic also accepted the plan. This made President Milosevic angry. He was furious, got up out of his chair, and said, "I'll give you your independent and sovereign Montenegro. I'll give you what for." It's difficult to interpret his words and the term he used, but it was a very serious threat, meaning, "I'll give you what for if you want an independent, sovereign Montenegro." So he got up. That's quite certain. He had to walk for 20 or 30 metres because there was the Macedonian delegation sitting in front of us, so he sort of threatened us for interrupting this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The meeting ended with all except the accused voting in favour of the plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. There was a vote. You either could state your views on the plan or there was a show of hands. Everybody raised their hands. It was only President Milosevic in his speech who rejected Lord Carrington's plan. And I would like to add that by doing so, he prolonged the war and opted for war instead of the peace offered by the international community, and brought the peoples -- the people of Serbia and all the other nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia to a great calamity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You returned to Montenegro. Did you return with Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, in due course, did Mr. Bulatovic change his position?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: He changed his position straight away, as soon as we returned to Montenegro. But may I be allowed to say the following? After the meeting, we had talks with President Tudjman, after the plenary meeting in The Hague, we also met with President Tudjman in The Hague as well. And I'd like to say a few words on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you can just give us the subject matter before we invite you to do so. What was the subject matter of the discussion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The establishment of peace between Montenegro and Croatia, to avoid war, and to discuss the question of the Prevlaka. And before we spoke of myself going to Zagreb, but now we were able to talk to President Tudjman. We tried to organise that, Kacic, myself, and President Tudjman, and President Bulatovic agreed that before they left for Zagreb and we left for Titograd that we should have a meeting and discuss the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the meeting fruitful? Was there a spirit of compromise with President Tudjman or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. We completely agreed, that is to say, President Bulatovic and President Tudjman agreed that they should not go to war and that the issue of the Prevlaka could be settled. And President Tudjman said if there were no war, then Prevlaka would not present a problem either. And he said if the relationship between Montenegro and Croatia was as it was during the times of Njegos and Ban Jelacic, then we would not even have to discuss the Prevlaka. But now that I'm at war, I don't have the right of handing over Prevlaka to you, but we'll discuss the matter and the Croatian Sabor or parliament will have to rule on that, and Dr. Kacic writes about that whole issue in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've probably got time to deal with deal with how it came about that Mr. Bulatovic changed his position immediately on return to Montenegro. Can you tell us first how you know how it came about that he changed his mind? Did he tell you? Did somebody else tell you? Did you discuss it with him? Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The very next day, as soon as we arrived in Titograd, Kostic and Jovic came to Titograd and Babic received them. President Milosevic had obviously sent them. And Bulatovic was told that he had to change his position. I did not attend that particular meeting. It was the leaders of Montenegro that attended the meeting, several of them. And Bulatovic was forced, he was actually forced to put his hand up and say he had made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see Kostic and Jovic in Podgorica, Titograd?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them myself, but I was told that they were there, and I knew that the meeting was being held in that same building, and judging by the police standing guard around the building, that there was an extraordinary situation taking place, as if war had started in Titograd. There were so many policemen there out on the Titograd streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you learn that it was they who'd persuaded him to change his mind? Did somebody tell you? If so, who?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me himself personally. President Bulatovic told me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he tell you the terms that were put to him by these two men?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: "Reject Lord Carrington's plan." That was it. And that a new Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. initiative should be adopted, and that initiative was known as the Belgrade initiative, which implied the organisation of a new state, a federal one, and Serbia and Montenegro would be the component parts. And so discussions started on the Belgrade initiative, and five days later, on the 23rd of October, a discussion was held in parliament on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... but did Mr. Bulatovic say what would happen if he declined to change his position on the Carrington Plan?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: He said to me that Jovic was categorical and said, "We'll bring in other people if you don't want to change your opinion and position." And in that situation, bringing in new people meant to lose your life, to bring in other people by saying that. Jovic -- that's what Jovic conveyed to me what Bulatovic said, that he said he would bring in other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now. Mr. Nice, how much longer do you anticipate being?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would like to say half an hour but I expect it will be 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Samardzic, would you be back, please, tomorrow morning at half past nine to continue your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of October, 2002, at 9.30 a.m. 22 23 24 25
